sections.text:
Numbers follows Israel from Mount Sinai to the edge of the promised land, a journey that takes about forty years. It opens with a census and marching orders, then tells of complaints, rebellion and unbelief. After spies bring a fearful report, the generation that left Egypt is told it will die in the wilderness.

The book ends with a new generation camped on the plains of Moab, counted again and ready to enter the land.

The English name comes from the two censuses in chapters 1 and 26. The Hebrew title means in the wilderness, which describes the book better. The very large numbers of people are debated: some take them at face value, others think the Hebrew word translated thousand may mean a clan or a military unit.

The New Testament uses these stories as both warning and encouragement, most clearly in 1 Corinthians 10 and Hebrews 3 and 4. The bronze serpent of chapter 21 is the picture Jesus uses of his own death in John 3. Readers also notice how patient God is in this book: judgment falls, and still he keeps the promise and brings the people on.
